meta.titre: Price Level Changes: inflation, price indices and who gains or loses
meta.sous_theme: Inflation, deflation, price index, causes, effects and control

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader in Douala notices that the bag of rice she bought for her shop a few years ago now costs much more, and so do transport, cooking oil and house rent. When most prices rise together and keep rising, the same 10,000 FCFA note buys fewer goods each year. Economists call this inflation, and they measure it with a price index. The GCE papers ask you to define these terms, to name the causes of inflation, to calculate an index or a rate, and to say who gains and who loses. A clear method for each of these tasks earns most of the marks.

items: A price is the amount of money paid for one unit of a good or service.
Money acts as a medium of exchange and as a measure of value.
A percentage change is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100.
Total demand in an economy is the spending of households, firms and the government.

sections.titre: Inflation, deflation and the price index
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms

- **Price level**: the average level of all prices in the economy.
- **Inflation**: a persistent rise in the general price level, so that each unit of money buys less. A rise in the price of one good, such as tomatoes in the dry season, is not inflation.
- **Deflation**: a persistent fall in the general price level.
- **Disinflation**: prices still rise, but more slowly than before, so the rate of inflation falls.
- **Price index**: a number that compares the average price of a basket of goods and services with its price in a **base year**, which is given the value 100. The **consumer price index (CPI)** uses a basket of what a typical household buys.

### Measuring the price level

$$\text{price relative} = \frac{\text{current price}}{\text{base-year price}} \times 100$$

$$\text{weighted index} = \frac{\sum (\text{weight} \times \text{price relative})}{\sum \text{weight}}$$

$$\text{rate of inflation} = \frac{\text{new index} - \text{old index}}{\text{old index}} \times 100$$

$$\text{purchasing power in base-year terms} = \text{money amount} \times \frac{100}{\text{index}}$$

The **weights** show how much of a typical budget is spent on each item.

### Causes and effects

| Cause | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Demand-pull | Total demand grows faster than output: more money in circulation, easy credit, higher government spending or lower taxes |
| Cost-push | Costs of production rise: wages, raw materials, fuel, imported inputs or taxes, and firms pass them on in prices |
| Imported | Prices of imported goods and inputs rise, and this spreads through the economy |

**Who loses:** people on fixed incomes such as pensioners, savers, lenders and workers whose wages lag behind prices. **Who gains:** borrowers, because they repay with money that has lost value, and owners of goods whose prices rise. Inflation also makes planning harder and can make exports less competitive.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When prices and weights of a basket are given
variantes.contenu_markdown:
1. For each item find the price relative: current price divided by base price, times 100.
2. Multiply each price relative by its weight.
3. Add the results and divide by the sum of the weights.

An index of 121 means that prices are on average 21% higher than in the base year. Always use the **old index** as the divisor when you find a rate of inflation.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks for measures to reduce inflation
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Match the remedy to the cause.

- **Monetary policy**: the central bank (for the franc zone of Central Africa, the BEAC) raises interest rates or limits credit so that spending falls.
- **Fiscal policy**: the government raises taxes or cuts its own spending to reduce total demand.
- **Supply-side measures**: encourage production, improve transport and allow more imports so that goods become more plentiful and costs fall.
- **Direct controls**: set maximum prices for essential goods, although shortages and black markets may follow.

Reducing demand suits demand-pull inflation; lowering costs suits cost-push inflation.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks what happens if the price level falls persistently
variantes.contenu_markdown: When prices keep falling, buyers delay purchases hoping for lower prices, firms earn less and may cut output and jobs, and the real burden of debts rises because loans must be repaid with money that buys more. A fall in the **rate** of inflation is not deflation: it is disinflation.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A household basket in a town contains three items. The prices (hypothetical) and the weights are:

| Item | Year 1 (base) price | Year 2 price | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rice, per kg | 500 FCFA | 600 FCFA | 50 |
| Fish, per kg | 1,000 FCFA | 1,300 FCFA | 30 |
| Cooking oil, per litre | 1,000 FCFA | 1,100 FCFA | 20 |

(a) Find the price relative of each item for Year 2.

(b) Calculate the weighted price index for Year 2.

(c) The index for Year 3 is 133.1. Calculate the rate of inflation between Year 2 and Year 3.

(d) A worker earns 242,000 FCFA a month in Year 2. Find the purchasing power of this pay in Year 1 prices.

etapes.justification: Divide the current price by the base price and multiply by 100.

etapes.action: Weight the price relatives and add.
etapes.justification: Items that take a larger share of the budget must count for more.

etapes.action: Divide by the sum of the weights.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Index for Year 2 $= \frac{12100}{100} = 121$, so prices are on average 21% above Year 1.

etapes.action: Find the rate of inflation from Year 2 to Year 3.
etapes.justification: Use the change in the index divided by the old index.

etapes.action: Find the purchasing power of the pay.
etapes.justification: Pay is deflated by the index to express it in base-year prices.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) 120, 130 and 110. (b) The Year 2 index is **121**. (c) The rate of inflation is **10%**. (d) The pay of 242,000 FCFA buys only what **200,000 FCFA** bought in Year 1, so its real value is much lower than the number suggests.

items.erreur_markdown: "Tomatoes became dearer this month, so there is inflation."
items.pourquoi_faux: Inflation concerns the general price level and a persistent rise. One price, or a seasonal rise, does not show it.
items.correction_markdown: State that inflation is a persistent rise in the **average** level of prices, measured by an index.

items.erreur_markdown: "The index rose from 120 to 132, so inflation is 12%."
items.pourquoi_faux: The rise of 12 is in index points, not in per cent. The change must be compared with the starting value.

items.erreur_markdown: "Inflation fell from 8% to 4%, so prices are now falling."
items.pourquoi_faux: A positive rate of inflation means prices are still rising, only more slowly. This is disinflation, not deflation.
items.correction_markdown: Prices still rise, by 4% a year. Deflation needs a negative rate of inflation.

items.pourquoi_faux: Borrowers repay in money that has lost value, and people whose incomes rise faster than prices are better off.
items.correction_markdown: Name both groups: lenders, savers and fixed-income earners lose, while borrowers and owners of rising assets can gain.

items.enonce_markdown:
The consumer price index of a country rises from 150 to 162 in one year.

(a) Calculate the rate of inflation.

(b) State what has happened to the purchasing power of money.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Rate $= \frac{162 - 150}{150} \times 100 = \frac{12}{150} \times 100 =$ **8%**.

(b) Prices are higher on average, so each unit of money buys fewer goods: purchasing power has **fallen**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A pensioner receives a fixed pension of 90,000 FCFA a month. Over some years the price index rises from 100 to 125 while the pension stays the same.

(a) Find the value of the pension in base-year prices at the end of the period.

(b) By what percentage has its purchasing power fallen?

(c) Explain why a borrower with a fixed loan would be in a different position.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $90000 \times \frac{100}{125} =$ **72,000 FCFA**.

(b) Fall $= \frac{90000 - 72000}{90000} \times 100 =$ **20%**.

(c) The borrower repays a fixed amount of money, but that money buys less than when it was borrowed, so the real burden of the debt falls and the borrower gains.

items.enonce_markdown:
In one year (i) the government raises its spending sharply, (ii) a trade union wins a large pay rise for factory workers and (iii) the price of imported fuel goes up.

(a) Say which of these are likely to cause demand-pull inflation and which cost-push inflation.

(b) Suggest one policy for each type.

(c) A man borrowed 2,000,000 FCFA when the index was 100 and repays 2,000,000 FCFA when the index is 160. Find the value of the repayment in base-year prices and the gain to the borrower, ignoring interest.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) (i) raises total demand: **demand-pull**. (ii) raises costs of production: **cost-push**. (iii) raises costs of production and is also an imported source: **cost-push**.

(b) Demand-pull: the central bank raises interest rates or the government raises taxes to reduce spending. Cost-push: supply-side measures such as improving transport or allowing more imports to lower costs.

(c) Value $= 2000000 \times \frac{100}{160} =$ **1,250,000 FCFA** in base-year prices. Gain $= 2000000 - 1250000 =$ **750,000 FCFA** in base-year prices.

items_markdown: Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level; deflation is a persistent fall; disinflation is a slower rise.
A price index compares a weighted basket with a base year set at 100: relative, weight, add, divide by the sum of weights.
Rate of inflation = change in index divided by the **old** index, times 100.
Demand-pull comes from excess total demand; cost-push comes from higher costs; match each policy to its cause.
Borrowers and owners of rising assets tend to gain; savers, lenders and fixed-income earners tend to lose.
